target.title: fix(commitments): avoid quadratic heartbeat session discovery
target.body:
Related: #105787

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes heartbeat commitment fan-out latency when many due commitments belong to one session. The existing path loads and expires the JSON store while holding the queue/file lock, releases that lock, then scans the returned in-memory records. For every qualifying due record it rescans the complete store to count recent sent commitments. The quadratic scan is outside the lock, but it delays heartbeat processing and increases heartbeat latency. Reported isolated medians were approximately 191 ms at 1,000 records, 847 ms at 2,000, and 2.28 s at 4,000.

## Why This Change Was Made

The commitments store now builds the rolling 24-hour sent-count map once per agent and reuses it for due-session discovery and single-session due selection. Due-window, snooze, expiry, daily-cap, ordering, limit, agent-scope, queue, and cross-process file-lock behavior remain on the existing path.

This is intentionally an interim JSON-store fix. OpenClaw's shared SQLite state schema already contains a commitments table and indexes, but making it canonical requires a separate JSON-to-SQLite migration/doctor contract and broader persistence coverage. That migration remains a follow-up rather than expanding this focused latency fix.

## User Impact

Heartbeat commitment discovery changes from repeated full-store counting to one aggregation pass plus the existing due-record scan. Large concentrated sessions therefore scale linearly with store size instead of quadratically, without changing which sessions are eligible for delivery.

## Evidence

- Store correctness coverage includes due windows, snoozes, rolling daily caps, agent scope, deterministic session-key ordering, expiry, and concurrent file-store updates.
- The concentrated-session regression uses 8,000 due records in one session and a production-like `limit: 10`, so the base implementation repeatedly rescans the store while the fixed implementation reuses one count map.
- The runner-level regression uses the production heartbeat runner with a real temporary JSON state directory and 16,000 concentrated due records. The model and channel boundaries are stubbed there for deterministic CI coverage.
- Focused validation, using the linked-worktree local fallback because Crabbox was unavailable:
  ```text
  node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/commitments/store.test.ts src/infra/heartbeat-runner.commitments.test.ts --reporter=verbose
  11 store tests passed; 14 heartbeat-runner tests passed.
  ```

### Real Gateway heartbeat proof

I also ran the actual built `dist/index.js gateway` in a fresh isolated state directory. The test seeded 16,000 pending due commitments plus one recent sent commitment, all concentrated in one Telegram session, then invoked the production Gateway `wake` RPC. The Gateway scheduler, heartbeat runner, JSON store, due-session selector, Telegram plugin dispatch, and delivery/status updates were real. The provider and Telegram Bot API were local HTTP fixtures, so the run was secretless and deterministic; no scheduler, store, runner, or channel-dispatch function was stubbed.

The baseline was built from the main checkout at `43901be298`, a descendant of the PR base `6c884691105b`; there were no changes under `src/commitments/` or `src/infra/heartbeat-runner.ts` between those refs. The PR run used `fcb249f4953485071e123b7cd2fce31f32ea96da`. Each line is one fresh Gateway process and one wake, with 16,000 records:

```text
baseline 43901be298:
REAL_GATEWAY_HEARTBEAT_PROOF {"store":"json","commitmentCount":16000,"channelSendCount":1,"runs":[{"iteration":1,"elapsedMs":33219,"pendingAfterRun":15998,"lastHeartbeat":{"status":"sent","to":"telegram:12345","durationMs":5509}}]}

PR fcb249f495:
REAL_GATEWAY_HEARTBEAT_PROOF {"store":"json","commitmentCount":16000,"channelSendCount":1,"runs":[{"iteration":1,"elapsedMs":15377,"pendingAfterRun":15998,"lastHeartbeat":{"status":"sent","to":"telegram:12345","durationMs":2909}}]}
```

This is a single matched before/after run, not a statistically stable benchmark. It includes cold Gateway startup and local fixture variance, but it demonstrates the real production process path: the PR completed the heartbeat in 15.4 s versus 33.2 s for the baseline, while both delivered one message and left the same 15,998 commitments pending. The one-off harness was local-only and is not part of the patch; the durable scaling proof is the concentrated-session regression above.

- `git diff --check`, `oxfmt --check`, and `oxlint` passed for the changed source/tests.
- Correctly invoked autoreview:
  ```sh
  .agents/skills/autoreview/scripts/autoreview --mode local
  .agents/skills/autoreview/scripts/autoreview --mode branch --base origin/main
  ```
  Local mode reported no uncommitted changes; the committed branch review reported no accepted/actionable findings.
- The configured Crabbox client could not provide remote execution because coordinator and broker authentication are missing (`accessAuth: missing`, `brokerAuth: missing`). GitHub checks for the current PR head completed with no failures; 41 checks were skipped, and the Real behavior proof check passed. The branch is behind current `origin/main` and still needs the normal rebase/current-head rerun before merge.

## AI-Assisted Disclosure

This PR was prepared with Codex and is AI-assisted. I reviewed the implementation, its callers, sibling selection path, persistence/locking behavior, tests, and the SQLite/Kysely storage contracts.
